extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of political philosophy and theory of government
extracted.subtask_description: A normative political-philosophy treatise arguing for the origins, limits, and ends of civil government, including accounts of natural law, property, punishment, slavery, and the state of nature/war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political power is 'a RIGHT of making laws with penalties of death, and consequently all less penalties, for the regulating and preserving of property, and of employing the force of the community, in the execution of such laws, and in the defence of the commonwealth from foreign injury; and all this only for the public good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish political power from paternal, masterly, conjugal, or lordly powers; it is legitimate only insofar as it makes laws for the public good and uses community force to execute them.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of nature (freedom and equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: All men are naturally in a state of 'perfect freedom to order their actions' and 'a state also of equality' where 'all the power and jurisdiction is reciprocal, no one having more than another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State of nature is not licence; natural freedom is bounded by the law of nature. Use this as baseline for assessing claims of natural subordination or inherited dominion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of nature (content and source)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of nature 'has a law of nature to govern it, which obliges every one: and reason, which is that law, teaches all mankind... that no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason is the measure of the law of nature; obligations exist independently of positive law and bind individuals in the state of nature and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to punish (individual execution of natural law)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature the execution of the law of nature 'is put into every man’s hands', so 'EVERY MAN HATH A RIGHT TO PUNISH THE OFFENDER, AND BE EXECUTIONER OF THE LAW OF NATURE.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment by individuals must be proportionate and aimed at reparation and restraint; this collective right is a ground for later delegating such power to magistrates in civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: One may punish 'so far as calm reason and conscience dictate, what is proportionate to his transgression, which is so much as may serve for reparation and restraint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitrary or excessive punishment is unlawful; the aim is reparation and deterrence. Officials or individuals exceeding proportion act beyond the law of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private right to reparation (distinct from public punishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the common right to punish, 'the injured party... has a particular right to seek reparation' and only he 'alone can remit' the satisfaction due to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magistrates may remit public punishment but cannot extinguish the private claim for satisfaction owed to an injured person.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of war (definition and causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of war is 'a state of enmity and destruction' arising when one declares 'a sedate settled design upon another man’s life' or attempts to bring another into absolute power without consent; force without right creates war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify state of war by declared design or use of force without legitimate appeal; distinguishes war from peaceful state of nature/society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of self-preservation and defensive killing
rubrics_metrics.description: It is lawful to kill one who makes war upon you or attempts to enslave you; similarly a thief using force to seize your goods may be killed because he 'puts himself into a state of war' by attempting to take your liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive lethal force is permitted when necessary to preserve life or prevent irreparable loss and where lawful remedies are not available in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between state of nature and state of war
rubrics_metrics.description: State of nature: living together according to reason without a common superior; State of war: force or declared design upon another’s person where there is no common superior to appeal to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate peaceful equality under natural law with the enmity of war; the presence/absence of a common judge and the use of unjust force are diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of civil society (remedy for inconveniences of state of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men put themselves into society and quit the state of nature to avoid the state of war and to have an authority 'from which relief can be had by appeal' so controversies can be decided and the continuance of war excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate government is justified as remedy for the defects of the state of nature (partiality, inability to secure impartial judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty under government (consent and rule of law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom under government means 'to have a standing rule to live by, common to every one of that society, and made by the legislative power erected in it' — not subjection to the arbitrary will of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate legislative authority must be by consent and produce known standing rules; arbitrary, unknown, or inconstant will undermines freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery (conditions and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery is 'nothing else, but the state of war continued, between a lawful conqueror and a captive'; no one can by compact 'put himself under the absolute, arbitrary power of another' except by forfeiture of life through serious crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary sale into absolute slavery is impossible since one cannot give what one does not possess (power over one’s life). Historical servitude often amounted to limited drudgery, not absolute slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisition of property by labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the world is given to mankind in common, 'every man has a property in his own person' and by mixing his labour with common things he makes them his property: 'whatsoever he removes out of the state that nature hath provided, and left it in, he hath mixed his labour with, and joined to it... and so they became his private right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation by labour is legitimate provided it leaves 'enough, and as good' for others; examples include gathering acorns, drawing water into a pitcher, digging ore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency constraint on appropriation ('enough, and as good')
rubrics_metrics.description: Property acquired by labour is just only 'at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation that deprives others of sufficient resources conflicts with the law of nature; this limits claims arising from individual appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason as arbiter and intelligibility of natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of nature is 'as intelligible and plain to a rational creature' as municipal laws; reason reveals duties such as mutual preservation and love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals to obscure tradition or authority must yield to clear principles discoverable by reason; policies should be justifiable to rational agents.
